subject: business-studies
topicDisplay: Decision Making To Improve Marketing Performance
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: During the 'maturity' stage of the product life cycle, sales typically:
options: Rise rapidly for the first time
Reach their peak and growth slows as the market saturates
questions.explain: At maturity sales plateau near their peak and growth slows because most potential customers already buy the product.

questions.q: The promotion element of the marketing mix is mainly concerned with:
options: Communicating with customers to inform and persuade them to buy
questions.explain: Promotion covers advertising, PR and sales methods used to inform and persuade customers.

questions.q: A 'dog' in the Boston Matrix is best described as a product with:
options: Low market share in a low-growth market
High share in a growing market
High share in a high-growth market
questions.explain: Dogs have low share in low-growth markets and are often candidates for divestment.

questions.q: Distribution (place) decisions concern:
options: The selling price of the product
The channels through which a product reaches the final consumer
questions.explain: Place covers the channels and intermediaries that move a product from producer to consumer.

questions.q: Cost-plus pricing involves:
options: Adding a fixed percentage mark-up to the unit cost of a product
Giving products away to gain share
questions.explain: Cost-plus pricing adds a mark-up to the unit cost to set the selling price.

questions.q: Price skimming is most appropriate when:
options: A product is a generic commodity with many substitutes
The firm wants the lowest possible margin
A new, innovative product has few competitors and customers willing to pay a premium
questions.explain: Skimming sets a high initial price to exploit early adopters of an innovative product before competitors enter.

questions.q: Competitive pricing (going-rate pricing) means a firm:
options: Sets prices in line with or close to those of its rivals
Sets prices well above the market to signal luxury
questions.explain: Competitive pricing sets prices around the prevailing market rate to stay in line with rivals.

questions.q: A firm using dynamic pricing (e.g. for flights or ride-hailing) is:
options: Charging one fixed price at all times
Varying prices in real time in response to changes in demand and supply
Refusing to use any digital data
questions.explain: Dynamic pricing adjusts prices in real time using data on demand, common in digital and e-commerce markets.

questions.q: A product with a PED of -0.4 is described as:
questions.explain: An absolute PED value below 1 means demand is price inelastic, so quantity responds little to price changes.

questions.q: In the Boston Matrix, a 'star' is a product with:
options: High market share in a high-growth market
High market share in a declining market
Low market share in a low-growth market
Low market share in a high-growth market
questions.explain: Stars combine high market share with high market growth and usually need investment to maintain their position.

questions.q: A penetration pricing strategy involves:
options: Charging different prices to different segments
Matching exactly the prices of all competitors
Setting a deliberately high initial price to skim early adopters
Setting a low initial price to gain market share quickly
questions.explain: Penetration pricing uses a low launch price to win customers and build market share rapidly.

questions.q: Targeting the over-65s with stairlifts is an example of segmentation by:
questions.explain: Age is a demographic variable, so targeting by age range is demographic segmentation.

questions.q: B2B marketing differs from B2C marketing chiefly because B2B:
options: Sells to final consumers for personal use
Sells to other businesses, with longer, more rational, relationship-based buying decisions
questions.explain: B2B targets other firms whose purchasing is typically rational, relationship-driven and involves larger, considered orders.

questions.q: Quantitative data differs from qualitative data in that quantitative data:
options: Is numerical and can be measured and statistically analysed
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical and measurable, whereas qualitative data captures opinions and reasons.

questions.q: E-commerce has most directly changed the 'place' element of the marketing mix by:
options: Removing the need for any product
Allowing firms to reach global customers directly through online channels
questions.explain: Online selling extends distribution (place), letting firms reach customers worldwide without physical outlets.

questions.q: If a 10% price cut leads to a 25% rise in quantity demanded, the PED is approximately:
questions.explain: PED = +25% divided by -10% = -2.5, so demand is price elastic.

questions.q: An 'extension strategy' in the product life cycle is used to:
options: Prolong the life of a product in the maturity/decline stage, e.g. by finding new uses or markets
Reduce the firm's product range to one item
questions.explain: Extension strategies such as restyling or new uses prolong sales when a product reaches maturity or decline.

questions.q: The marketing mix for a service business is most commonly extended from the 4 Ps to the 7 Ps by adding:
questions.explain: The 7 Ps add People, Process and Physical evidence to the original Product, Price, Place and Promotion.

questions.q: Product portfolio analysis is mainly used to:
options: Decide a single product's price only
Assess the balance of a firm's range of products and guide investment decisions
questions.explain: Portfolio analysis, e.g. the Boston Matrix, reviews the mix of products to inform investment and marketing strategy.

questions.q: Which is a primary purpose of branding?
options: To differentiate the product, build customer loyalty and allow premium pricing
To avoid the need for any promotion
To make the product price elastic
questions.explain: Strong branding differentiates a product, fosters loyalty and supports charging a premium price.

questions.q: Price elasticity of demand (PED) is calculated as:
options: %change in price divided by %change in quantity demanded
Change in total revenue divided by change in price
%change in quantity demanded divided by %change in price
questions.explain: PED = percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.

questions.q: In the Boston Matrix, a product with high market share in a low-growth market is classified as a:
questions.explain: High share in a low-growth market makes a product a cash cow that generates steady cash with little new investment.

questions.q: If a product is price inelastic, a firm wishing to increase total revenue should:
options: Raise the price, since quantity demanded falls less than proportionately
questions.explain: For inelastic demand a price rise lowers quantity by a smaller proportion, so total revenue increases.

questions.q: An advantage of intuitive decision-making over scientific decision-making is that it:
options: Can be faster and useful where data is unavailable or markets change rapidly
questions.explain: Intuition allows quick decisions when reliable data is lacking or conditions move too fast for full research.

questions.q: Market segmentation is best defined as:
options: Setting one price for all customers
Dividing a market into distinct groups of consumers with similar characteristics or needs
questions.explain: Segmentation splits a market into groups (e.g. by age or income) so marketing can be tailored to each.

questions.q: A limitation of relying on secondary market research is that:
options: It can never be obtained quickly
It is always more expensive than primary research
It may be out of date or not specific to the firm's exact needs
It is always biased toward the firm
questions.explain: Secondary data was gathered for other purposes, so it can be outdated or not perfectly relevant to the firm.

questions.q: Niche marketing differs from mass marketing because it:
options: Targets the whole market with a standardised product
Targets a small, specific segment with a specialised product
Always uses lower prices than mass marketing
questions.explain: Niche marketing focuses on a narrow, specialised segment rather than the broad market that mass marketing serves.

questions.q: Scientific (data-driven) marketing decision-making relies primarily on:
options: Evidence from market research and quantitative analysis to reduce risk
questions.explain: Scientific decision-making uses research evidence and analysis to reduce the risk of marketing choices.

questions.q: A USP (unique selling point) helps a business by:
options: Giving a clear point of differentiation that makes its product stand out from rivals
Removing the need to set a price
questions.explain: A USP differentiates a product, helping it stand out and reducing direct price competition.

questions.q: The 'design mix' balances which three elements?
questions.explain: The design mix balances function, aesthetics and cost (economic manufacture) when designing a product.
